title: An audience of one
hook: enough are few, enough is one, enough is none

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was the crowd, which shapes us more than we notice. Your line was what I bring home.

A post gets four likes and you feel faintly foolish for sharing it. A song you worked on for months gets a hundred plays. A talk you prepared gets a half-empty room. There's a number under nearly everything we make now. Seneca didn't have the number, but he knew the itch. Right after warning Lucilius about the crowd, he ends his seventh letter with three small sayings about how big an audience really needs to be.
screen: `FOUR LIKES.` → `A HALF-EMPTY ROOM.` → `AN AUDIENCE OF ONE.`

segments.voice: Lucilius might object: then what did I learn all this for, if no one will hear it? Seneca's first answer: you learned it for yourself. Then he gives three sayings, like three small gifts. First, Democritus, the old philosopher of atoms: one person counts as much as a whole people to me, and a whole people as much as one. The size of the audience doesn't change the worth of the work. Second, a craftsman, though Seneca says it's uncertain who. Asked why he took such pains over an art very few would ever appreciate, he answered: a few are enough for me. One is enough. None is enough. The work was worth doing well for its own sake. Third, Epicurus, the founder of a rival school, writing to a friend who studied with him: I say this not for the many, but for you; we are each a big enough audience for the other. Seneca's point, gathering all three: don't let the pleasure of being praised by many pull you back into the crowd. Most of the good in the world is done for an audience of one: a meal for a sick friend, a letter, a careful repair, a child's question answered properly. Nobody counts those. They count anyway.
screen: `WHO WILL SEE MY WORK?` · `DEMOCRITUS: ONE IS A WHOLE PEOPLE.` · `A FEW, ONE, EVEN NONE IS ENOUGH.` · `EPICURUS: AUDIENCE ENOUGH.` · then, large: `ONE IS ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: Picture one person who will benefit from something you do today: a coworker, a parent, a kid with homework, a patient, a neighbor. See their face, and picture doing that one thing really well, as if they were the whole audience, because they are. Let that be enough.
Democritus. The old philosopher of atoms, quoted by Seneca: one person counts as much as a whole people to me, and a whole people as much as one.
Your line: one is enough. A few, one, or even none. Day four hundred forty-two.

screen: `DAY 442 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: ALL MINE IS WITH ME.`

original.note: Latin: one is enough, from the saying in Seneca's seventh letter.

what it means: Seneca says one person, or even no one, is enough reason to do good work; chasing a crowd pulls you back into it.
what a scholar hears: the three sayings come from a materialist philosopher (Democritus), an unnamed craftsman and Epicurus; Seneca borrows freely across schools.

chat.meaning: Democritus, the craftsman and Epicurus agree: a few, one, even none is enough. The audience's size doesn't change the work's worth.

Democritus.meaning: the old Greek philosopher of atoms

Epicurus.meaning: a Greek founder of a rival school; Seneca quotes him often

Lucilius.meaning: Seneca's friend, to whom the moral letters are written
